discipline_framing: The subconscious-influence discipline of advertising — how sensory inputs, colors, emotional triggers, and design elements shape purchasing behavior before the consumer realizes it, spanning consumer neuroscience measurement, perception and attention science, multisensory marketing, affect and memory systems, and the ethics boundary separating legitimate subconscious design from neuromyth and manipulation.
audience: Aspiring advertising creatives, brand designers, UX and packaging specialists, media planners, and research-literate marketers who want the empirical grounding behind sensory and emotional design decisions — and the skepticism to distinguish real neuroscience from vendor hype.
sources: Phil Barden, Decoded: The Science Behind Why We Buy — the practitioner bridge applying dual-process decision science to marketing stimuli, value, and framing
Patrick Renvoisé & Christophe Morin, Neuromarketing: Understanding the Buy Buttons in the Brain — applied stimulus design from contrast, tangibility, and emotion principles

McClure, Li, Tomlin, Cypert, Montague & Montague (2004), Neural Correlates of Behavioral Preference for Culturally Familiar Drinks, Neuron — the canonical Pepsi-Paradox fMRI study anchoring brand-effect neuroscience
Dan Hill, Emotionomics — the role of emotional states and facial-response measurement in advertising effectiveness
Kenneth Holmqvist et al., Eye Tracking: A Comprehensive Guide to Methods and Measures — the methodological standard for attention measurement
Binet & Field, The Long and the Short of It, with the IPA Effectiveness databank — evidence base for emotional-reach versus rational-persuasion advertising effects
NMSBA (Neuromarketing Science and Business Association) — buying guides, code of conduct, and vendor standards for neuromarketing research practice
pitfalls: Neuromyth laundering: dressing ordinary preference research in brain-imaging imagery and borrowed authority, buying credibility without adding measurement value
Vendor-report credulity: commissioning black-box studies whose methods, baselines, and sample sizes never face scrutiny, then defending unreplicable claims in strategy meetings
Subliminal hyperbole: believing mind-control myths about hidden messages while ignoring the real, bounded effects of supraliminal priming, salience, and fluency
Tool fascination: selecting fMRI or EEG for questions that eye tracking, implicit tests, or well-designed surveys answer better, faster, and cheaper
Scanner-to-market leap: treating neural activation in artificial lab conditions as purchase prediction without behavioral validation, effect-size realism, and field testing
